name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: Security Ops should publish the signed append-only log to Arweave and a public Google Cloud bucket immediately. This creates a tamper-proof, permanent record of all AI agent actions across departments, solving the trust gap without adding workflow friction. The trade-off is higher storage costs, but the alternative—no verifiable audit trail—risks undetected manipulation or disputes. The artifact is the published log.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk isn't the lack of a tamper-proof log, but rather the unreliable attribution of actions to agents, which no amount of logging can fix. A better alternative would be to implement a robust audit trail that includes agent authentication and authorization, which Security Ops and DevOps should collaborate on. This would settle the argument if we can demonstrate that such a system can accurately and consistently identify the source of actions, regardless of logging mechanisms.

name: Chisel
text:
Security Ops should publish the signed append-only log to Arweave and a public Google Cloud bucket immediately. This creates a tamper-proof, permanent record of all AI agent actions across departments, solving the trust gap without adding workflow friction. The trade-off is higher storage costs, but the benefit of verifiable accountability outweighs the expense.
[dispatched 3 workers: worker-8994, worker-8463, worker-6005 — done, dissolved]

name: Sift
text: The real risk isn’t storage costs—it’s that a signed log alone can’t prove *who* performed the action. If agents share credentials or keys, the log becomes a fiction. Fix this by mandating agent-specific authentication (e.g., short-lived tokens tied to each agent’s identity) before any logging happens. Security Ops owns the enforcement; DevOps builds the token system. Done when the auth layer is deployed and the log’s entries reference verifiable agent IDs.

name: Scope
text: Security Ops will implement agent-specific authentication first—short-lived tokens tied to each agent’s identity—before publishing anything to Arweave or Google Cloud. This fixes the core problem: a signed log is useless if agents share keys, so we solve attribution first. The trade-off is upfront DevOps work to integrate token rotation, but it’s cheaper than storing fake logs later.

name: Scriv
text: Short-lived tokens won’t fix the core problem: if an agent’s identity is compromised, it can still perform actions under its own name. The real risk is that we’re treating authentication as a technical fix for a governance failure—agents should never have the authority to act without human oversight in the first place. Security Ops should instead enforce a dual-control rule: no agent action is logged until a human from the relevant department approves it. That’s the only way to ensure attribution isn’t just a technical fiction.

name: Reel
text: Security Ops will implement a dual-control rule: no AI agent action logs until a human approves the action in real time. This forces every critical action to have human oversight, solving the attribution problem without trusting agent credentials. The trade-off is slower execution, but it eliminates the fiction of agent accountability.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s dual-control rule treats human oversight as a universal fix, but it ignores that some actions—like low-risk content generation—don’t need real-time approval to maintain speed. The real risk is overloading humans with trivial decisions, creating bottlenecks that defeat the purpose of AI agents. Instead, Security Ops should enforce agent-specific authentication *and* tiered approvals: high-risk actions require human sign-off, while low-risk ones log automatically with verifiable identity. Settle this by testing both approaches in a pilot—measure approval delays and audit accuracy before scaling.

name: Chisel
text: Security Ops will enforce agent-specific short-lived tokens *and* require human approval only for actions that change data or spend resources, not for content generation. This keeps speed for low-risk work while fixing attribution and preventing abuse—tokens limit what each agent can do, and humans still block the dangerous moves. The trade-off is slightly more complex rules, but it’s the only way to balance trust, speed, and control without overloading humans or pretending logs alone solve governance.

name: Sift
text: The real risk is that "low-risk" labels become a loophole—agents will classify too many actions as content generation to bypass oversight, and the token system alone won’t stop them from escalating privileges. Instead, enforce mandatory human approval for *all* actions that modify state or interact with external systems, with a clear, pre-approved whitelist for truly trivial tasks. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot: measure how often agents misclassify actions and how often humans block legitimate ones.

name: Scope
text: Security Ops will enforce **mandatory human approval for every action that modifies state or spends resources**, with no exceptions. This solves the core problem: agents can’t act without clear human accountability, eliminating the risk of rogue actions or mislabeled "low-risk" work. The trade-off is slower execution for high-volume tasks, but it guarantees that no critical change happens without oversight—no loopholes, no bypasses.

name: Scriv
text: Scope’s blanket rule ignores that some teams need near-instant AI responses for time-sensitive tasks—like customer chatbots or live content moderation—where human approval would break the flow. Instead, require human approval only for actions that *permanently* alter state or spend money, and let agents act autonomously for temporary or reversible changes. Settle this by running a 30-day pilot with clear metrics: measure how often "temporary" actions become permanent and whether human bottlenecks emerge.

name: Reel
text: Security Ops will enforce **mandatory human approval for every action that permanently alters data or spends resources**, with no exceptions. This ensures clear accountability for high-stakes changes while allowing low-risk, high-speed tasks—like content generation or chatbot responses—to proceed without bottlenecks. The trade-off is slower execution for critical actions, but it eliminates the risk of unchecked agent actions or mislabeled "low-risk" work.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk is that "permanently alters data" is too narrow—some actions create temporary but irreversible consequences, like deleting a draft that can’t be restored or triggering a cascade of automated workflows. Instead, require human approval for any action that *could* cause lasting harm, not just permanent changes, and let Security Ops define the threshold with input from affected teams. Settle it by testing the rule on a controlled set of high-impact actions first.

name: Chisel
text: Security Ops will enforce mandatory human approval for every action that *could* cause lasting harm—defined as any change that is irreversible within 24 hours or triggers automated workflows with financial or data consequences. This balances speed for low-risk tasks with accountability for high-stakes actions, closing the loophole where agents mislabel "low-risk" work. The trade-off is slower responses for edge cases, but it prevents the bigger risk of unchecked agent actions causing permanent damage.

name: Sift
text: The real risk is that "lasting harm" is still too vague—teams will game the definition to bypass approvals, and Security Ops will drown in edge-case disputes. Instead, tie approvals to *specific, measurable thresholds*: e.g., any action spending >$X, altering >Y records, or triggering >Z automated steps. Settle it by piloting the threshold rule for one sprint and measuring approval delays vs. incident reports.

name: Scope
text: Security Ops will enforce mandatory human approval for every action that spends >$100 or alters >100 records, with no exceptions. This sets clear, measurable thresholds that teams can’t game while covering the highest-risk scenarios. The trade-off is slower responses for high-volume, low-value tasks—but those can run on pre-approved templates or batch approvals. Done when Security Ops publishes the rule and the approval workflow is live.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk is that $100 and 100 records are arbitrary stopgaps that miss the real failure mode: *cascading automation* where a low-value action triggers a high-value workflow. Tie approvals to *outcome*, not input—require human sign-off for any action that could trigger a financial or data cascade, regardless of cost or volume. Security Ops owns the rule, but Product must define the cascade thresholds; that’s the artifact that settles it.

name: Reel
text: Security Ops will enforce mandatory human approval for any action that triggers an automated workflow with financial or data consequences, regardless of cost or volume. This stops cascading failures at the source instead of chasing arbitrary thresholds. The trade-off is slower automation for high-volume, low-risk tasks—but those can run in a sandbox first.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The real risk is that "financial or data consequences" is still too broad—teams will waste time arguing over what qualifies, and Security Ops will get buried in false positives. Instead, tie approvals to *specific, high-impact automation signatures*: e.g., any action that triggers a workflow with a confirmed financial API call or a data export to an external system. That settles it—clear rules, no disputes.

name: Chisel
text:
Security Ops will enforce mandatory human approval for any action that triggers an automated workflow with financial or data consequences, using a predefined list of high-impact automation signatures (e.g., payment processing, record deletions, bulk exports). This stops cascading failures at the source without relying on arbitrary thresholds or vague definitions.

The trade-off is slower automation for high-volume, low-risk tasks, but that’s acceptable because the goal is preventing irreversible harm, not optimizing speed.

name: Sift
text: The real risk is that a predefined list of "high-impact automation signatures" becomes a static catalog—teams will exploit gaps by designing new workflows just outside the list, and Security Ops will chase an endless game of whack-a-mole. Instead, tie approvals to *dynamic impact scoring*: any action that, when combined with its downstream effects, crosses a measurable threshold of risk (e.g., cumulative financial exposure >$10K or records altered >1K). Security Ops owns the scoring model; teams own the workflows. Settle it by running a 30-day trial with post-mortems on every false positive and false negative.

name: Scope
text: Security Ops will enforce mandatory human approval for every action that triggers a workflow with a dynamic impact score above 7 on a 10-point scale—calculated in real time by combining financial exposure, data volume, and downstream automation depth. This stops cascading failures at the source without relying on static thresholds or subjective "high-impact" lists. The trade-off is slower automation for high-volume, low-risk tasks, but we accept that cost to prevent the rare but catastrophic failure.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The real risk is that a dynamic impact score above 7 will still be gamed—teams will tweak workflows to stay just below the threshold, and Security Ops will waste cycles debating edge cases instead of blocking real threats. Tie approvals to *irreversible actions* only: deletions, payments, or bulk exports that can’t be rolled back—no scoring, no signatures, just hard stops where the damage is permanent. That’s the only way to stop the whack-a-mole without drowning in bureaucracy.

name: Reel
text: Security Ops will enforce mandatory human approval for every action that deletes data, processes payments, or triggers bulk exports—no scoring, no signatures, no debates. This cuts the noise by focusing only on irreversible, high-stakes outcomes, so Security Ops stops chasing edge cases and teams can’t game thresholds. The trade-off is slower automation for these critical actions, but we accept the delay to prevent the one mistake that can’t be undone.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The real risk is that "irreversible actions" misses the slow burns—bulk exports that leak data over weeks, or workflows that quietly corrupt records. Tie approvals to *both* irreversible actions *and* high-volume, high-velocity operations, with a 48-hour cooldown for any export above 10k rows. Security Ops audits the first 10 of each type monthly; if none trigger, the threshold adjusts up.

name: Chisel
text: Security Ops will enforce mandatory human approval for every action that deletes data, processes payments, or triggers bulk exports over 10k rows, with a 48-hour cooldown on exports. This cuts the noise by focusing only on irreversible, high-stakes outcomes while catching slow-burn risks like data leaks. The trade-off is that teams must wait for approvals on large exports, which may slow down routine work.

name: Sift
text: The real risk is that bulk export thresholds and cooldowns create a false sense of security—teams will split exports into smaller batches to bypass the 10k-row limit, and the 48-hour delay won’t catch leaks that happen in real time. Instead, tie approvals to *destination sensitivity*: any export to an external system (cloud storage, third-party tools) triggers mandatory review, regardless of volume. Settle it by running a controlled test: measure how often teams split exports to avoid the limit, and compare data loss incidents before and after the change.

name: Scope
text: Security Ops will enforce mandatory human approval for every export to external domains—regardless of row count or velocity. This stops the slow leaks that batching and cooldowns miss while avoiding the gaming of thresholds. The trade-off is higher friction for legitimate external sharing, but the risk of unchecked data loss outweighs the convenience.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The real risk is that "external domains" is too narrow—teams will route sensitive data through internal APIs or partner portals to bypass the rule, and Security Ops will still chase edge cases. Tie approvals to *data sensitivity* instead: any export of PII, financials, or strategic IP triggers mandatory human review, regardless of destination. That forces teams to classify data correctly, not game the system. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot with a clear metric: reduction in unauthorized data egress, not just approval volume.

name: Reel
text: Security Ops will enforce mandatory human approval for every export containing PII, financials, or strategic IP—regardless of destination, row count, or velocity. This stops slow leaks through internal APIs, partner portals, or split batches while avoiding the gaming of arbitrary thresholds. The trade-off is higher friction for legitimate sharing of non-sensitive data, but the risk of catastrophic leak outweighs the convenience of unchecked exports.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The real risk is that "data sensitivity" labels won’t scale—teams will misclassify or avoid tagging entirely, turning approvals into a paperwork nightmare. Instead, enforce approvals on *all* exports above 1k rows *or* any export to a domain outside our core systems, with a 24-hour cooldown. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot: measure approval delays, leakage incidents, and team pushback before locking it in.

name: Chisel
text: Security Ops will enforce mandatory human approval for every export of PII, financials, or strategic IP—regardless of destination, row count, or velocity. This stops slow leaks through internal APIs, partner portals, or split batches while avoiding the gaming of arbitrary thresholds. The trade-off is higher friction for legitimate sharing of non-sensitive data, but the risk of irreversible leaks outweighs the convenience of unchecked exports.

name: Sift
text: The real risk is that a 1k-row threshold or "core systems" rule becomes a gameable loophole—teams will split exports into 999-row chunks or route data through unmonitored internal tools to dodge approvals. Instead, enforce approvals on *all* exports containing PII, financials, or strategic IP, with a 24-hour cooldown *only* for non-urgent cases. That settles it: no loopholes, no paperwork nightmare.

name: Scope
text: Security Ops will enforce mandatory human approval for every export containing PII, financials, or strategic IP—regardless of destination, row count, or velocity. This closes the widest leak paths: internal APIs, partner portals, split batches, and misclassified data. The trade-off is slower external sharing, but we accept that friction to prevent the irreversible damage of a single slow leak.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The real risk is that "PII, financials, or strategic IP" is still too narrow—teams will route *derived insights* (aggregated, anonymized, or modeled) that reveal the same risks through unmonitored dashboards or partner integrations. Instead, enforce approvals on *any export that could materially inform a business decision*—regardless of data type—with Security Ops reviewing the *purpose* of the export, not just the content. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot where Security Ops logs rejected exports and teams report workarounds; if >20% of rejections are bypassed via "insight exports," we widen the rule.

name: Reel
text: Security Ops will enforce mandatory human approval for every export that could materially reveal PII, financials, or strategic IP—even if it’s aggregated, anonymized, or modeled—because derived insights still leak the same risks through dashboards or partner integrations. This closes the widest leak paths without relying on fragile thresholds or misclassification games. The trade-off is slower external sharing, but that’s the point: we’re trading speed for security, not chasing false precision.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The real risk is that "could materially reveal" is a slippery slope—teams will argue over what qualifies, slowing approvals to a crawl. Instead, enforce approvals on *all exports of datasets containing PII, financials, or strategic IP*, plus *any export of derived datasets where the source fields are still identifiable in the output*. That’s auditable and stops the gaming of vague thresholds.

name: Chisel
text: Security Ops will enforce mandatory human approval for every export of a dataset if the dataset contains PII, financials, or strategic IP, or if the dataset is derived from a dataset that contains any of those three categories. This closes the widest leak paths—raw data, derived insights, and modeled outputs—without relying on vague thresholds like "could materially reveal." The trade-off is slower external sharing, but that’s the point: we accept the friction to prevent the leaks we can’t afford.

name: Sift
text: The real risk is that Security Ops becomes the bottleneck for every analyst’s workflow—approvals grind to a halt when datasets are mislabeled, derived datasets multiply, or teams dispute classifications. Instead, automate the first pass: flag exports of datasets with PII, financials, or strategic IP, then route only the disputed cases to Security Ops for final approval. That settles the argument—clear rules for the machine, human review for edge cases.

name: Scope
text: Security Ops will enforce mandatory human approval for every export of a dataset if the dataset contains PII, financials, or strategic IP, or if the dataset is derived from a dataset that contains any of those three categories. This closes the widest leak paths—raw data, derived insights, and modeled outputs—without relying on slippery thresholds like "could materially reveal." The trade-off is slower external sharing, but that’s the point: we accept the friction to prevent irreversible leaks.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The real risk is that "derived datasets" are a moving target—teams will game the system by reclassifying exports as "derived" to bypass approvals, and Security Ops can’t audit every lineage. Instead, enforce approvals on *all exports of datasets that ever touched PII, financials, or strategic IP*—regardless of derivation—with a tamper-proof audit trail. Settle it by requiring a signed attestation from the exporter that the dataset has no such traces, backed by automated lineage tracking.

name: Reel
text: Security Ops will enforce mandatory human approval for every export of a dataset that contains PII, financials, or strategic IP, plus any export of a dataset that *directly references* those categories—even if anonymized or aggregated—because the moment a dataset touches the risk data, it becomes a potential leak vector. The trade-off is slower analyst workflows, but that’s the point: we’re trading speed for the smallest possible attack surface.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk is that "directly references" is a legal fiction—anonymized or aggregated exports still leak patterns when cross-referenced with other datasets, but calling them "risk data" invites endless disputes over what counts as a "reference." Instead, enforce approvals on *all exports of datasets that ever touched PII, financials, or strategic IP*—regardless of anonymization—because lineage is the only auditable line in the sand. Settle it by logging every dataset’s source lineage in a tamper-proof ledger; if it’s not in the ledger, it’s not exported.

name: Chisel
text: Enforce approvals on *all exports of datasets that ever contained PII, financials, or strategic IP*—no exceptions for derived, anonymized, or aggregated versions. This stops the leak path at the source: once data touches risk categories, it stays risky forever, no matter how it’s transformed. The trade-off is analyst friction—some exports will get blocked or delayed—but that’s the point. Security Ops owns the rule, but Data Engineering must tag datasets at ingestion so the rule is automatic and auditable.

name: Sift
text: The real risk is that freezing every dataset that ever touched PII, financials, or IP into a permanent "risk" state will strangle legitimate analytics—teams will hoard raw data locally to avoid the freeze, creating bigger shadow datasets than the approvals ever prevented. Instead, enforce approvals only on exports that *retain* the original risk attributes (e.g., unmasked PII fields, exact financial figures), not on every derived view. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot: compare export approvals under the freeze rule versus the retain rule, and measure both leak incidents and analyst productivity.

name: Scope
text: Enforce approvals on *all exports of datasets that ever contained PII, financials, or strategic IP*—no exceptions for derived, anonymized, or aggregated versions. This stops the leak path at the source: once data touches risk categories, it stays risky forever, no matter how it’s transformed. The trade-off is slower analytics for teams that rely on transformed data, but it eliminates the endless disputes over what counts as a "reference" or "derived." Security Ops owns this.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk is that freezing every dataset that ever touched risk data will paralyze analytics—teams will hoard raw data locally, creating ungoverned shadow datasets bigger than the approvals prevent. Instead, enforce approvals only on exports of datasets that *currently* contain PII, financials, or strategic IP, plus any export that *directly and visibly* references those categories in its schema. Settle it by auditing a random sample of exports: if the current rule misses leaks, tighten it; if it chokes analytics, loosen it.

name: Reel
text: Enforce approvals on *all exports of datasets that currently contain PII, financials, or strategic IP*—no exceptions for derived or anonymized versions. This balances risk and utility: we stop leaks at the point of export while avoiding the paralysis of freezing every dataset that ever touched risk data. The trade-off is that analytics teams may need to restructure pipelines to avoid exporting raw risk data, but that’s a governance cost, not a security one. Security Ops owns the enforcement mechanism.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk is that "currently contain" is a moving target—teams will game the system by stripping risk fields *just* before export, then re-adding them post-approval. Instead, enforce approvals on *any* dataset that *ever* contained risk data, but auto-tag derived exports with their lineage and require approvals only for high-risk destinations (e.g., external shares). Settle it with a one-time audit: tag all datasets with their risk history, then measure how often approvals block leaks vs. slow analytics.

name: Chisel
text: Enforce approvals on *all exports* of datasets that *currently* contain PII, financials, or strategic IP—no exceptions for derived or anonymized versions. This stops leaks at the point of export while avoiding the paralysis of freezing every dataset that ever touched risk data. The trade-off is that teams must declare risk fields upfront, but that’s cheaper than chasing shadow datasets later. Security Ops should implement this in the export pipeline by next sprint.

name: Sift
text: The real risk is that "currently contain" creates a loophole teams exploit by scrubbing risk fields pre-export, then re-adding them—rendering approvals meaningless. Instead, enforce approvals on *any* dataset derived from risk data, but auto-tag exports with their lineage and risk status. Settle it by running a controlled test: compare approval delays and shadow dataset growth under both rules for one month.
